Solve One Weighted Least Squares Step

Source: R/iwls.R
iwls_solve.Rd

Returns the increment \(\delta\) solving \((H + S)\delta = u\) by the requested decomposition.

Usage

iwls_solve(
  pieces,
  u,
  how,
  damp = 0,
  frozen = integer(0),
  tol = NULL,
  floor = 1e-08
)

Arguments

pieces

A list with R, C and A, as iwls_pieces() builds it. Which of the three are present depends on how.

u

The right-hand side \(X'g - S\beta\), a numeric vector of length p.

how

The decomposition: "qr", "svd" or "chol".

damp

The Levenberg damping \(\lambda\), a single non-negative number. 0, the default, is the plain scoring step.

frozen

Positions that the caller holds at their current values, an integer vector. They are dropped from the system exactly as a coordinate whose curvature is not finite is, so the step is that of the problem reduced to the rest. The default is empty.

tol

The tolerance of the factorization, as the solver carries it: the pivoted QR tolerance for how = "qr", the relative cut of the singular values for how = "svd" (NULL for the default cut), and unused for "chol". The default is NULL.

floor

The relative floor of the eigenvalues of an assembled matrix that is not positive definite, as pd_repair() takes it. The default is 1e-8.

Value

A list of five:

delta

the increment, a numeric vector of length p, zero in every held coordinate.

rank

the rank of the system solved, an integer.

route

which decomposition was used: the one requested, or "qr->chol" or "svd->chol" when the augmented route fell back to the assembled matrix with its eigenvalues floored.

held

the positions dropped from the system, an integer vector, empty when every coordinate was free.

dropped

the positions that the pivoted qr() left out as aliased, an integer vector, empty on every other route.

The two families of route

"qr" and "svd" decompose the augmented matrix \([R;\, C]\), whose cross-product is the penalized information, so \(X'X\) is never formed and the condition number is never squared. That route needs the per-observation curvature to be positive definite and the penalty positive semidefinite. Where either fails, as with an observed Hessian far from the optimum or a non-convex penalty, there is no square root to take: the step falls back to the assembled matrix with its eigenvalues floored, and records the fallback in route as "qr->chol" or "svd->chol".

"chol" factors the assembled information directly, after flooring the eigenvalues of a matrix that is not positive definite.

Levenberg damping

damp adds \(\lambda I\) to the system, which shortens a coordinate in proportion to how little curvature it has. A coordinate whose diagonal is \(d\) is shortened by \((d + \lambda)/d\), so that a coordinate with a small diagonal is shortened more than one with a large diagonal: a differential shrink, which a scalar step length cannot give. The damping is zero unless a step has failed.

On the augmented route the damping enters as further rows of the augmented design, so the QR route keeps its conditioning; on the assembled route it is added to the diagonal. The matrix added is the identity. A damping proportional to \(\mathrm{diag}(K)\) would shrink every coordinate alike and leave the disparity exactly where it was.

A coordinate at a boundary is held

Where a parameter has reached the clamp with which its link keeps it strictly inside its bounds, the family's curvature there is zero or NaN, and that coordinate cannot be moved by any step. Those coordinates are dropped from the system and the rest is solved, which is the active set that the boundary defines; the step stays a descent step for the reduced problem. Coordinates in frozen and coordinates with a non-finite right-hand side are held in the same way.

Holding them keeps a single boundary coordinate from preventing the others from moving: a NaN in one entry of the curvature would otherwise make the whole step zero.

On the augmented route a coordinate is held when its column of the square-root design or of the penalty factor has a non-finite entry. On the assembled route the test is on the diagonal of the curvature. A boundary coordinate makes its entire row non-finite, cross terms included, so a test over whole columns would mark its neighbors too and hold coordinates that can move. After the diagonal test, the columns of the reduced matrix are tested again, and the test repeats until every column is finite.

See also

iwls_pieces() for the input, iwls() for the solver argument that this function serves.
